title: Trie Structures
description: Discover tries: tree-like structures optimized for fast prefix matching, autocomplete, and dictionary lookups.

data.text: A trie, pronounced 'try,' is a tree where each edge represents a character and each path from the root to a node spells a prefix of one or more stored words. Tries excel when you need fast prefix-based search, such as autocomplete or spell checking.
Each node contains a set of child nodes, one per possible character. Many implementations also include a boolean flag that marks whether the path from the root to that node completes a valid word.

data.title: Trie node contents
items: A map or array of child references keyed by character.
An end-of-word flag to mark completed entries.
Optional payload for word metadata such as frequency or definition.

data.content: Inserting and searching words in a basic trie.

data.text: Insertion, search, and prefix checks all depend on the length of the word, not on how many words are stored. This makes tries attractive for large dictionaries where the number of words dwarfs the average word length.

data.title: Where tries shine
items: Autocomplete suggestions as a user types.
Spell checkers that need prefix-aware corrections.
IP routing tables that match longest prefixes.
Search engines that support prefix expansion.

data.title: Memory awareness
data.text: Tries can use more memory than hash tables if the alphabet is large and words are short. Compressed tries, also called radix trees, reduce this overhead by collapsing single-child nodes.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Tries organize characters along paths from root to leaf.
Lookups depend on word length, not total dictionary size.
They are ideal for prefix-based tasks such as autocomplete.
Compressed variants save memory when the dataset is large.
data.takeaway: Tries turn the problem of string search into a fast, character-by-character walk down a tree.
